name: Beth Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Beth, thanks for talking to me. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to give me both your public answer and your private one. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the tax team at a regional firm, about a hundred and twenty people across three offices, and I do personal tax returns for people who own small companies. Think a couple who run a printing shop and pay themselves a salary and dividends, and I work out the most sensible way to do that. I get in at half eight, clear emails, then it's returns, calls with clients and chasing missing paperwork. On Saturday mornings I volunteer at a free tax clinic in a community centre, which is honestly my favourite part of the week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a client realises they've been overpaying and you can fix it. What wears me out is the firm since it was bought by a private equity fund last year, an investment fund that buys firms to sell them on. Everything's now billable hours and targets, and my team lead Marta looks exhausted all the time. I use an AI tool now and then to tidy up client emails, but that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, now can we talk about the actual problem, which is the fund squeezing everyone. At the clinic I'd tell the volunteers the tax system is still too complicated for normal people, AI or not. Online I'd probably share something about how the hype served investors more than workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the pressure I already have doesn't go anywhere. The fund wants the firm worth more in three years, so the targets keep rising whatever the software does. My job's safe, I think, but I'm not sure I want it on these terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job but quietly start looking at other firms by the spring, maybe a partner-owned one. I'd use the email tool a bit more, since it saves me twenty minutes a day. And I'd keep paying extra off my mortgage, because owning more of the flat feels like freedom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, honestly. Not scared of losing work, just tired of the place. A bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your day would the routine automation touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pulling numbers from bank statements and filling the standard boxes on the return. That's maybe a fifth of my time. The fund would just hand the saved time back to me as more clients, not as an early finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure you want the job on these terms. What would you change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want targets that count the time you spend explaining things to a scared client. At the moment that's my time, not the firm's. Marta fought for that and lost.

say: I'd say the real problem is the **private equity** owner squeezing staff.
I'd tell clinic volunteers the **tax system** is still too complicated for normal people.
think: My job looks **safe**, but the fund's **targets** will keep rising regardless.
I'm not sure I want this job on the firm's **new terms**.
do: Look at **partner-owned firms** quietly by the spring.
Use the **email tool** more to save twenty minutes a day.
Keep making **extra payments** off the flat's mortgage.
feel: **Tired** of the place rather than afraid of losing work.
A bit **flat** about the years ahead.
S0.quote: The fund would just hand the saved time back to me as more clients, not as an early finish.
fieldNote: Her unease comes from an **existing pressure**, the new private equity owner, not from AI.
She frames saved time as something the **owner** captures, not staff.
The free **tax clinic** is where her values and her energy really sit.

steps.text: Apply to partner-owned tax firms by the spring
Use the AI email tool daily for client letters
Pay an extra amount off the flat mortgage monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when we need a union in professional jobs, not just factories. I'd post about it, and I'd say it at the clinic too, because the people we help will be hit by cheaper, worse advice. At work I'd say it to Marta and maybe one or two others, carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my team of eight becomes five, and I'm average at this job, so I could easily be one of the three who go. The fund would love this, because it means more clients per head. I'd probably be fine finding something, since there are firms everywhere, but every firm would be doing the same cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tax software's AI features properly in the first three months, once I'd seen Marta use them. I'd push toward the advice side, the calls with business owners, because that's what software is worst at. And I'd join a union for finance staff and get two colleagues to join with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I've got savings and a flat, so I'm not going under. It's more watching the ground move under people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for Marta to use the features first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've watched new tools come in here and break in January, when it matters most. If Marta trusts it after a season, I'll trust it. I'm not a first-week person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin team who scan and sort the paperwork, and honestly the people at the clinic. A lot of them are cleaners and care workers who do a bit of self-employed work on the side. If advice gets automated, they'll get the cheapest version.

say: I'd say professional jobs need a **union** now, not just factories.
I'd warn that clinic users will get **cheaper, worse** advice.
think: My team of **eight** could become five, and I could be cut.
Other firms would make the **same cuts**, so moving wouldn't fully protect me.
do: Learn the tax software's **AI features** within three months.
Move toward **advice calls** with business owners.
Join a **finance union** and bring two colleagues along.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, thanks to savings and the flat.
**Sad** watching the ground shift under people I like.
S1.quote: I think my team of eight becomes five, and I'm average at this job, so I could easily be one of the three who go.
fieldNote: She expects **real cuts** to her team and sees herself in the firing line.
Her **steady** style shows: she'll adopt tools once her team lead trusts them.
Her worry extends to **low-paid clinic clients** who'd get the cheapest automated advice.

steps.text: Learn the tax software's AI features within three months
Ask Marta to move her onto advice calls with owners
Join a finance staff union and sign up two colleagues

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest handover of wealth in history and we didn't vote for it. I'd be at whatever protest happened, and I'd be posting a lot. At work there'd be a lot of people crying in the kitchen, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job's gone within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner, because the fund would move fastest of anyone. My work is all screens and phone calls. The robots taking three more years means nothing to me, because nothing I do needs hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the mortgage down hard in the two years before it lands, so the flat costs as little as possible to keep. I'd look for work that's mostly hands and people, maybe as a support worker for the council while the robots are still years off. And I'd volunteer for whatever political campaign was fighting for public ownership of these systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the air's been let out. Angry, scared, and a bit numb. I keep picturing Marta clearing her desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you protect first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, every time, because without the flat I'd be back at my parents'. I'd cut the car, the gym, the holiday with my sister. Food and the flat, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents helped with the deposit, and I'd feel I'd wasted it on a career that lasted six years. My dad would say it's not my fault. I'd still feel it.

say: I'd call it the biggest **handover of wealth** that nobody voted for.
I'd join **protests** and post about it a lot.
think: My job goes within **a year**, with the fund moving fastest.
The **robot delay** means nothing, since my work needs no hands.
do: Pay the **mortgage** down hard in the two years before.
Seek **support work** for the council while robots are still years off.
Volunteer for a campaign for **public ownership** of AI systems.
feel: Haunted by picturing my **team lead** clearing her desk.
S2.quote: My parents helped with the deposit, and I'd feel I'd wasted it on a career that lasted six years.
fieldNote: She is sure the **private equity** owner would cut fastest of all.
Protecting the **flat** is her first and firmest priority.
Guilt toward her **parents** sits alongside anger at the system.

steps.text: Overpay the flat mortgage every month before 2028
Apply for council support worker jobs
Volunteer for a campaign for public ownership of AI
Cut the car, the gym and the holiday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and I want to see a plan for workers by next year, not a report. I'd keep saying it at the union and at the clinic. Online I'd share anything practical, like who's offering free retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to make one proper move, not two. I'd be thirty-two, still young, with no kids, so I'm luckier than most. But the job itself goes, and I don't believe the firm would warn us properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start an evening course in social work or counselling, something where the person in the room is the point. I'd keep working full-time to keep paying the mortgage down. By year three I'd want to have switched, before the stampede.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more like a deadline than a cliff. I can work with deadlines, I'm an accountant. Still not nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social work or counselling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the tax clinic, people don't thank me for the maths. People thank me for sitting with them while they cry about a tax bill. I think I'm better at that than at returns, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said before the stampede. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If everyone at a desk sees it coming, the courses fill up in year four. I'd rather be the annoying one who switched early. My sister will call me dramatic, but she's a lawyer, so she should be worried too.

say: I'd demand a real **plan for workers** within a year, not a report.
I'd share news of **free retraining** online and at the clinic.
think: Five years allows **one proper move**, not two.
At **thirty-two** with no kids, I'm luckier than most people.
do: Start an **evening course** in social work or counselling.
Keep working **full-time** to keep paying down the mortgage.
Switch careers by **year three**, before the rush.
feel: **Anxious**, but it feels like a deadline, not a cliff.
Some **confidence** from being good at working to deadlines.
S3.quote: At the tax clinic, people don't thank me for the maths. People thank me for sitting with them while they cry about a tax bill.
fieldNote: She discovers her real strength may be **care**, not calculation.
Her plan is about **timing**: switch before others crowd the courses.
Five years shifts her from alarm to a **deadline mindset**.

steps.text: Start an evening course in social work or counselling
Keep working full-time and overpaying the mortgage
Move into a care or counselling job by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently, so if it goes badly, that's a political choice. I'd push for a shorter working week and a share of the gains for staff. At work I'd say it in team meetings, not just to Marta.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get seven or eight more years in tax, maybe more on the advice side. Then it's gone, at thirty-seven or so. That's a long time to plan, but a long time to dread it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in tax for now and get good at the AI tools once they're proven, to stay useful. I'd do the counselling qualification part-time over three years, without rushing. And I'd join the party campaigning for a shorter working week, and actually go to meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but quieter. Like knowing a big exam is far off. You can sleep, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the decade change anything personal, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd stop putting off a partner and a family, weirdly. I've been waiting until work settles down. With ten years, I'd stop waiting for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said dread. What would you do with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk about it at the clinic, oddly. Half the volunteers are retired and they've been through factories closing. They'd tell me how they got through it, and that would help more than any article.

say: I'd say a bad outcome with ten years' notice is a **political choice**.
I'd push for a **shorter working week** and staff sharing in gains.
think: I'd likely get **seven or eight** more years in tax.
A decade is long enough to plan but also long enough to **dread**.
do: Learn the **AI tools** once proven, to stay useful in tax.
Do a **counselling qualification** part-time over three years.
Join the party campaigning for a **shorter week**.
feel: Still **anxious**, but quieter, like a distant exam.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to do this decently, so if it goes badly, that's a political choice.
fieldNote: Her blame falls squarely on **political choices**, not on the technology itself.
The long runway nudges her to stop **postponing** personal life.
She'd lean on the **retired volunteers** who lived through factory closures.

steps.text: Learn the firm's AI tax tools once they're proven
Study for a counselling qualification part-time over three years
Join and attend meetings of the shorter-week party

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because the fund would cut first and think later. What would help is free retraining with a wage, and the gains taxed and shared, not sent to investors. Honestly, a union contract that says you get a year's notice would help me sleep tonight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the software. That's the whole question for me. If the firm's AI belonged to the people who do the work, half my worry would go.

headlineQuote: If the firm's AI belonged to the people who do the work, half my worry would go.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** tax accountant doing returns for small company owners at a firm bought by private equity.
She owns a flat with a **parental deposit** and volunteers at a free tax clinic on Saturdays.
Even in AI Plateau she is **uneasy**, worn down by the fund's rising targets.
She adopts AI tools **once proven** and turns to unions and politics to share the gains.
In the AGI pictures she would move toward **counselling or social work**, sooner the faster it comes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the private equity owner would cut staff first and think later.
whatWouldHelp: **Free retraining** with a wage, and AI gains **taxed** and shared.
A union contract guaranteeing a **year's notice** before cuts.
